verbatim: The fingerprint machinery and capability ladder and all other machinery are supposed to work in harmony with each other. There is no reason why any of this should no either work, work in the envisaged way, and work in harmony with everything else in the harness as a whole. The singe unifying goal of this project has been that of a science/STEM calculator, problem entered into the system and a definitive, reliable, repeatable answer out, just as is the case with any normal calculator. Does it just stay in that upper league, do we create a new upper league for the more capable models, and how do we tell at any given time which models ae more and which are less capable than others, especially from a cold start at the beginning of an experiment? My initial instinct, without having read anything that has been written so far is in a cold start condition to at first give all the models a very hard randomly generated maths problem to solve, and then only promote the top performing models to the ‘top league’. The top performers would be those who solved the problem the fastest, using tools and writing proofs/falsifiers to validate/disprove the maths problem, and who did so in the most overall cost effective way. This could give you your initial ‘rankings’ I presume? Then for models that performed less well you could assign them a less complex maths problem, and then assess the best performing models in that less demanding position, and you could theoretically continue to do this until the best overall ranking of all available models and the best and most efficient allocation of available resources had been achieved? But surely this is a question that has been asked in computer science before? I cannot be the only person in the history of computer science who has ever wondered what the best and most efficient way to allocated available resources, CPU/GPU, memory and storage capacity and cost (although cost needn’t be a primary factor at this time, as it might be difficult to always reliably calculate, beyond perhaps a reported estimate) unless a researcher ran all models through a single resource like OpenRouter, which of course (like me) a researcher may not always be inclined, or be able to do.) So time for a little, or perhaps a lot of reading I think. How does my (possibly rather crude idea stack up against the competition? Are we attempting to reinvent the wheel? How do other project that us a similarly distributed compute model like Folding@Home, Seti@Home, Einstein@Home and others (although you shouldn’t just restrict your reading to projects of this nature) tackle the same problem? Obviously it doesn’t make sense to pitch a little desktop PC, against an entire vast supercomputer/server stack, so how exactly should we tackle this? That said, ultimately CDSFL was always envisaged from the outset to be capable of running on similar principles to these projects, although ultimately preferably we could go one step further and require no central server at all (except that required by the models participating in an experiment themselves), and that as well as running in standard configuration, as we are doing and have done from the outset of this project, the system should be capable of running in peer to peer mode too (a bit like bit torrent). We had a lot of discussion about this quite early on in the project, but I don’t know if any work was done, or if anything was ever actually built, or if it is even still useful if it was built? So as well as doing external research, rather than have me repeat the whole conversation again, please do some deep archaeology on these specific discussions, to see if there is anything there that might help resolve our problem, or at least where on our design journey these capabilities should be built on our roadmap/runway, if indeed they are not already?

title: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t k
verbatim: Something I have been mulling over all night too is again the cold start issue in any given experiment. Since we can’t know immediately what resources we have, at the outset of an experiment, or how well the models might perform, or what their rankings should be, the only solution I could potentially come up with was indeed again taken from our football analogy. Here during winners cup draws, or the European league, smaller less capable teams can sometimes be randomly picked to run against much bigger, much more capable teams/players. Sometimes this can indeed be done via a coinflip, but most often its done by randomly selecting names of ‘clubs’ from a silk bag. So at the beginning no capability of any team or player is simply assumed, They are simply randomly selected and through each successful wining round, the winning teams/players then play against each other in a matched pair, then the process repeats itself until only the top ranking players and teams are pitched against each other. I don’t know if this together with my previous observation resolves anything? Butin the real world, this usually ends up with only the best top players and teams matched against each other, where other lesser players/teams sit further down in the league table. The problem is when we push the football analogy too far, and start saying thee should be x number of ‘leagues’, and y number of players, or payers should have special names like football stars that get them more recognition than others, or when we start talking about should thee not just be individual players, but actual whole teams? No none of that needs to be true, surely, because first we are not actually playing football, so there is no requirement for us to follow exactly the rules that football follows, and secondly the football analogy is just that an analogy. We shouldn’t have out code littered with football references,, or talk of ‘defenders’, or strikers, or even ‘leagues’, as such or anything like that. The purpose of using an algology is simply to help us decide how things in a complex environment of exactly the kind we are considering might be best allocated and utilised. Not to turn CDSLF into a literal (if slightly overengineered) version of Fifa Football manager 2027! So in reality there should probably be no distinction between models participating in an experiment other than a ‘ranking number’, or some equivalent, or better methodology that might arise from your own work, or your research. As I said previously, although quite a lot of water has flowed under the bridge since I first said it earlier yesterday, the only things that should denote a model’s ranking in any given experiment is derived/demonstrable capability, either above that. Or below that of is peers. With each direction determining its ranking during an experimental run. So we just need to find a way that resolves these problems comprehensively. That’s all.

title: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of a
verbatim: 300 attempts for a single model to solve any given problem is clearly vastly much too much! For the entire majority of almost every experiment we have ever run, this would almost certainly cause the needle of a models ranking to barely move and to probably never move at all. Ae you even checking if these numbers make any practical sense before writing them? To go back to our football analogy, but to not hyper-focus on it in many football tournaments, when teams are drawn against each other, they usually get two attempts, or two matches to play each other. If one team loses they usually get knocked out of the tournament (but under our no benching rule, that clearly can’t happen, so all this means is a model stays in the same position it started in). But since this is not actual football as I said (and I don’t actually like football anyway) we don’t need to follow exact football rules), so although it is slightly arbitrary and not measured, maybe we could give models 3 chances to resolve a problem before their ranking is calculated, or perhaps 2 really is enough? I guess the only way to figure this out is to decide if this is a useful extension of this analogy or not, or of there is perhaps a better solution awaiting that we simply haven’t considered yet? At one point in your output, I though I had read that the model’s recommendation was that there should be 3000 leagues (or some other crazy number like this). The point in any case is that the number of models used may eventually be entirely arbitrary. It could be 5.or 6, or 70, or 500, or 1. (Which of course, has nothing to do with model names, or setting an arbitrary limit on the ladder of 2, or any limit at all.) The simplest understanding of this is, problem in (by the researcher, who then waits) -> problem computed efficiently by the models) -> solution out. title: Free, cheap, model name, setting an arbitrary limit on ‘how far the ladder can climb’ as I said are not meaningful consi
verbatim: Free, cheap, model name, setting an arbitrary limit on ‘how far the ladder can climb’ as I said are not meaningful considerations. The only thing that impacts capability in the schema, should be capability. If a more expensive model can do a better, more effective job – especially with a particularly complex problem that they are better suited for, and possibly do so more inexpensively (although that is clearly not the only consideration, since there is still no point handing a cheaper model work it is unlikely to be able to do), then they should be assigned this work, based on measured performance/capability fingerprints and the other machinery of the schema. If a lesser model would suffice for less complex problems, then the schema should prefer them for this work. We already have something like this in our simulated runners (where the lessons learned in simulated experiments will in due course be carried over to our real runners), and partially in the real runners, where Haiku functions on some of the less demanding jobs (as a classifier) in the schema. We would simply be taking the lessons learned more broadly here and what we know in this regard already, and applying these lessons to the whole schema. That is one of the problems I asked Astra to look at. But does the combined approach you recommended earlier today do this? Does it do it well? Is there a better way?

title: Same question as before. But with one observation. A ladder is bidirectional. It goes both up and down. So if a weaker m
verbatim: Same question as before. But with one observation. A ladder is bidirectional. It goes both up and down. So if a weaker model gets better at doing a job (say for example if a vendor releases an updated version, it should be able to climb the routing ladder, based on its demonstrated improvement in capability. Conversely if a stronger model proves less able, say due to some technical glitch or other, it should be able to climb down the ladder to a point where it again becomes effective. But what we need to guard against is simply counting when a model is successful as an ‘improvement in capability’. The only measure of improved capability is actual observed capability (and the converse.) But that said you were very enthusiastic in your assessment just immediately pre-your last compaction, that a combination of my approach (no max rungs on the ladder) and Astra’s approach provided the optimum outcome in all cases. But then you didn’t mention this again after you compaction. So how does this combined approach solve the tension exactly?
